newsitem.title: UK: Britain angry, others softer on strikebound France.
newsitem.headline: Britain angry, others softer on strikebound France.

text.p: Britain said on Monday it had protested to France over a week-old strike by French truck drivers that has blocked highways and borders, but most European governments seemed sympathetic to Paris' predicament.

British Transport Secretary George Young voiced concern at the plight of stranded British lorry drivers and the financial damage to small haulage operators in a weekend letter to his French counterpart, Bernard Pons, officials said.
"Hundreds of British haulers remain stranded in various parts of France," Young wrote. "I naturally hope that this action can be brought to an end as soon as possible."
He said some British drivers had been stuck for six days and there would be many claims for compensation for damage to perishable cargoes and for loss of earnings.
Spain protested to the French embassy last week about the impact of the strike on Spanish truckers and exports, saying European Union states must guarantee the free movement of goods.
French truck drivers blockading motorways and fuel depots allowed some Spanish and Portuguese colleagues to go home at the weekend after they had spent days stranded penniless in France.
On Monday, a senior official in the six-month-old conservative Spanish government voiced sympathy with Paris and said there would be no further pressure from Madrid.

"The French government is the one that's enduring the strike. President (Jacques) Chirac has enough on his plate with people being unable to fill up at petrol stations. He doesn't need to get calls from Spain," the official said.
Germany took a similarly understanding view, although the strikers stepped up their action on the Franco-German border on Monday, closing off five key crossings to goods vehicles.

"No foreign government can help," a German official said. "It is a matter for the French government itself to deal with the unions. That would be the same case if there were a strike in Germany. No foreign government could get involved."
The French Foreign Ministry said it was in contact with EU partners about problems affecting foreign drivers.
Asked about official protests, a spokesman told reporters: "The right to strike exists in all European Union countries."

Britain's Road Haulage Association said more than 700 British vehicles were estimated to have been caught up in the blockade by French drivers seeking higher wages, shorter hours and earlier retirement.

"This is a combination of industrial anarchy and official incompetence," said Sydney Balgarnie, a spokesman for the industry group. "There are drivers who have been trapped for some days and they are running out of money and food."
The British truckers want the French authorities to provide certificates to substantiate any claims for compensation.
The British Foreign Office has advised people not to travel to France with trucks but it is difficult to find alternative routes especially to reach Spain and Portugal.
The French truckers reinforced their campaign on Monday, with blockades at the ports of Calais and Boulogne -- major routes for ferries to Britain.
The problems for British drivers have been exacerbated by the closure of the Channel Tunnel last week because of a fire. The tunnel has been reopened to freight trains only.
